### Problem: Distinct Numbers {#sec-hash-p3-a}

::: {.p-statement}
Given $n$ numbers ($1 \le n \le 2\cdot10^5$, $1 \le x_i \le 10^9$), print the number of **distinct** values.

Source: [CSES 1621 · Distinct Numbers](https://cses.fi/problemset/task/1621){.solved}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
"Distinct" is the hash set's reason to exist: insert everything, read the size. The sorting alternative exists too, and is worth knowing because it is the guaranteed version and generalises to "sorted distinct list".
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Sort, then count changes.** Sort and count positions where $b_i \ne b_{i-1}$: $O(n\log n)$ guaranteed, $O(1)$ extra beyond the copy.
2. **Insert into a set.** $\Theta(n)$ expected, one line — `len(set(a))`.

**Invariant.** After processing $[0,i)$, the set holds exactly the distinct values of that range.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Sort and count the changes

::: {.form-next}
Duplicates sit next to each other after sorting, so the distinct count is one plus the number of *adjacent changes*. $O(n\log n)$, deterministic, and it also hands you the distinct values themselves if you need them — something the size of a set cannot do.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def distinct_sorted(a):
    if not a:
        return 0
    b = sorted(a)
    return 1 + sum(1 for i in range(1, len(b)) if b[i] != b[i - 1])
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

int distinctSorted(vector<int> a) {
    if (a.empty()) return 0;
    sort(a.begin(), a.end());
    return (int)(unique(a.begin(), a.end()) - a.begin());
}
```
:::

#### Insert everything, read the size

::: {.form-next}
A set *is* "the distinct values seen so far" — the count question becomes `len(set(a))`. One pass, $O(n)$ expected, and the invariant is the definition of the structure.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-distinct-numbers
def distinct(a: list[int]) -> int:
    return len(set(a))


for _ in range(800):
    a = [random.randint(1, 15) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 20))]
    assert distinct(a) == distinct_sorted(a)

assert distinct([3, 2, 1, 3, 3]) == 3
assert distinct([5]) == 1
assert distinct([1, 1]) == 1
print("distinct OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false); cin.tie(nullptr);
    int n; cin >> n;
    unordered_set<long long> s;            // identity hash: fine without adversarial tests;
    s.reserve(2 * n);                      // with them, add a custom hash or sort (@sec-hash-anti)
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) { long long x; cin >> x; s.insert(x); }
    cout << s.size() << '\n';
}
```
:::
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Sort and count the changes** is $O(n\log n)$ guaranteed, $O(1)$ space beyond the array (or in place on a copy). **Insert everything, read the size** is $O(n)$ expected time and $O(n)$ space — with the usual asterisk that an adversarial set of keys can degrade it (@sec-hash-anti). At $n = 2\cdot10^5$ the sort is just as affordable, and it cannot be attacked, so it is the safe default in C++.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- All equal: $1$. Single element: $1$. Empty input (not allowed here, but cheap to handle): $0$, which is why the sorted form checks for it.
- Values to $10^9$: rules out a frequency array (@sec-arr-p5); a set or sorted scan is the answer.
:::

::: {.practice}
- [LC 217 · Contains Duplicate](https://leetcode.com/problems/contains-duplicate/){difficulty="Easy"} — `len(set(a)) < len(a)`; membership mid-scan instead of size at the end.
- [CF 1454B · Unique Bid Auction](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1454/B){rating="800"} — count every value, then find the smallest value that occurs exactly once and report its position.
:::
